cards.title: What is a **microcontroller** (MCU)?
cards.body:
A single chip that holds a CPU core, program memory (flash), working memory (SRAM) and peripherals, so it can run a program with very few outside parts.

A typical MCU contains these blocks, all on one piece of silicon:
- CPU core
- on-chip **flash** (program storage) and on-chip **SRAM** (working memory)
- a bus matrix that connects the blocks
- clock and reset circuits
- general-purpose input/output (GPIO) pins that software can drive high or low or read
- timers, serial ports such as UARTs (simple two-wire serial links), and an analog-to-digital converter (ADC)
- a DMA controller and a debug port

Key idea: everything the program needs is inside the package. Add power, decoupling capacitors and the sensors or actuators, and it runs.

Watch out: an MCU is not a tiny laptop. It usually has no MMU, no full operating system such as Linux and no external DRAM, and its program lives in its own flash.

cards.title: What is a **peripheral** on a microcontroller?
cards.body:
A hardware block on the chip, outside the CPU core, that software controls through memory-mapped registers: a GPIO port, timer, UART or ADC, for example.

The CPU configures a peripheral by writing its control registers and checks it by reading its status registers. Once started, the peripheral works on its own: a timer keeps counting and an ADC keeps converting without the CPU executing a single instruction for them.

Example: once a pin is set up as an output, writing a 1 to its bit in the GPIO output register makes the pin go high. The pin voltage changes because dedicated hardware reacts to that write.

Watch out: peripheral registers are not ordinary memory. Reading one can clear a flag, and the value can change by itself, so accesses must go through `volatile` pointers.

cards.title: What is a **system-on-chip (SoC)**, and how does an MCU fit that label?
cards.body:
A chip that integrates processor core(s) and most of the other blocks of a system on one die; an MCU is a small SoC, though "SoC" usually means a bigger chip whose main memory is external DRAM.

A **die** is one piece of silicon. A phone or single-board-computer SoC packs several CPU cores, a GPU, memory controllers and often a modem or radio onto one die, but its gigabytes of DRAM sit in separate chips. An MCU usually puts its flash and SRAM on the same die as the core.

Why it matters: the label tells you little, so ask what is inside. On-chip program memory and no external DRAM means MCU-style design. A memory controller for external DRAM and a memory management unit (MMU) for a full operating system means an application-class SoC.

Watch out: vendors call MCUs with a radio built in "wireless SoCs". Judge the part by its memory and its processor core, not by the marketing word.

cards.title: How does a **processor core** differ from the microcontroller chip built around it, and what is **IP licensing**?
cards.body:
The core is the processor design (pipeline, registers and closely tied blocks such as the interrupt controller), often licensed from a company such as Arm; the chip is a vendor's product that wraps that core with flash, SRAM, a bus matrix, clocks, peripherals and pins.

In **IP licensing** a company sells a reusable design block (its "intellectual property") instead of chips. Arm designs cores such as the Cortex-M family and licenses them to chip makers, which build MCUs around them. Arm does not sell the MCU chips.

Example: two vendors can both ship a Cortex-M4 part. The CPU runs the same instructions on both (apart from optional blocks the vendor picks, such as a floating-point unit) and has the same kind of interrupt controller, but flash size, peripherals, pin layout and peripheral register addresses differ, because the vendor designed everything outside the core.

Watch out: "Cortex-M4" tells you the CPU and its instruction set, not the peripherals. Firmware that touches GPIO or timers does not port between vendors without rewriting; read the vendor's own manual.

cards.title: Roughly what clock speed, flash and SRAM does a mainstream Cortex-M4F microcontroller such as the STM32F407VG have?
cards.body:
$168\,\mathrm{MHz}$, $1\,\mathrm{MiB}$ of flash and $192\,\mathrm{KiB}$ of SRAM.

The STM32F407VG datasheet quotes a Cortex-M4 with FPU (a hardware floating-point unit, hence "M4F") at up to $168\,\mathrm{MHz}$, up to $1\,\mathrm{MB}$ of flash and $192\,\mathrm{KB}$ of SRAM ($112 + 16 + 64$, where the $64$ is a separate core-coupled block). ST writes "Mbyte" and "Kbyte" for binary sizes, so in this course's notation these are $1\,\mathrm{MiB}$ and $192\,\mathrm{KiB}$. It also has $4\,\mathrm{KiB}$ of backup SRAM.

Example: a laptop with $16\,\mathrm{GiB}$ of RAM has about $87{,}000$ times more memory than this chip's $192\,\mathrm{KiB}$, yet the chip can run an RTOS (a small real-time operating system), a USB stack and a small neural network.

Tip: use this part as your mental anchor for a "mid-range" MCU. Small parts have tens of KiB of flash and a few KiB of SRAM; flagship parts have megabytes and hundreds of MHz.

cards.title: Trade-off: a battery-powered sensor must react to an event within microseconds and run for months. Do you pick a microcontroller or an application processor?
cards.body:
A microcontroller, because it wakes in microseconds, responds with predictable timing and can sleep at a tiny fraction of the power an application processor idles at.

An **application processor** is a CPU with an MMU, built to run a full operating system such as Linux from external DRAM. It boots in seconds, runs at GHz clock speeds and usually draws well over a milliwatt even when idle.

An MCU runs one program or a small RTOS straight from flash and starts from reset almost at once. Low-power MCUs sleep at currents on the order of a microamp.

The other side: pick the application processor when the product needs Linux services (a file system, a full network stack, a display toolkit), camera pipelines or gigabytes of memory. Many products use both: an MCU handles real-time work and wake-ups, and an application processor sleeps until needed.

Watch out: raw MHz is a poor guide. A $48\,\mathrm{MHz}$ MCU can meet a microsecond deadline that a $1\,\mathrm{GHz}$ Linux system misses, because the OS scheduler adds unpredictable delay.

cards.title: Trade-off: do you pick the smallest part that fits today's firmware, or the next larger member of the same product family?
cards.body:
The next larger, pin-compatible family member when the firmware may still grow and the price gap is small; the smallest part only when the firmware is frozen and volume makes every cent count.

A **product family** is a set of parts with the same core and peripheral design but different flash, RAM and pin counts, often pin-compatible so a bigger part can drop onto the same board.

Why: running out of flash or RAM late in a project forces a firmware squeeze or a board respin, which costs far more than the price difference. A bigger part also leaves room for features, a larger model and a second firmware copy for safe updates.

The other side: at millions of units, a few cents per chip is real money, and a frozen design can safely use the smallest part. Choose a family whose smaller members you can move down to later.

Tip: a common rule of thumb is to keep some spare flash and RAM (often 20 to 30 percent) at the first design review, then pick the part from there.

cards.title: What is **Thumb-2**, and why does it matter for flash size?
cards.body:
An instruction set that mixes 16-bit and 32-bit instructions, giving near-full speed with compact code; Cortex-M processors run only Thumb-family instructions.

Common operations, such as adding two registers or loading a small constant, have 16-bit encodings. Operations that need more bits, such as a 16-bit immediate or a long branch, use 32-bit encodings. The decoder handles both in the same stream.

Example (assembled for a Cortex-M3): `movs r0, #1` is 2 bytes (`0x2001`) while `movw r5, #0x1234` is 4 bytes (`0xf241 0x2534`).

Why it matters: **code density** is how few bytes of machine code a program needs. Denser code fits in a smaller, cheaper flash and needs fewer flash reads, which saves energy.

Watch out: Cortex-M0 and M0+ implement a smaller Thumb subset with only a handful of 32-bit instructions, so they need more instructions for the same job than M3 and above.

cards.title: What is the **Cortex-M0+**?
cards.body:
Arm's smallest, most energy-efficient Cortex-M core: an Armv6-M design with a two-stage pipeline, no FPU, no DSP instructions and no hardware divide.

It is still a 32-bit core, with 32-bit registers and a 4 GiB address space, but it executes a deliberately small Thumb subset to keep silicon area and power low. It has no floating-point unit (FPU: hardware for `float` arithmetic) and none of the DSP (digital signal processing) instructions that speed up multiply-accumulate loops.

Why it matters: low area means low cost and low leakage, so the M0+ suits coin-cell sensor nodes, simple motor or LED controllers and the housekeeping brains inside larger chips.

Watch out: small does not mean weak at control tasks. It means weak at heavy arithmetic: each divide or floating-point operation becomes a library routine, and multiply-heavy loops get no DSP help.

cards.title: What does the **Cortex-M4** add over the Cortex-M3?
cards.body:
DSP instructions (fast multiply-accumulate and SIMD operations on packed 8- and 16-bit values) and an optional single-precision FPU.

The Cortex-M3 implements Armv7-M. The M4 implements Armv7E-M, which is Armv7-M plus these digital-signal-processing extensions. **SIMD** (single instruction, multiple data) means one instruction works on several small values packed into one 32-bit register. A **floating-point unit (FPU)** is a hardware block that does floating-point add, multiply and similar operations in a few cycles instead of running a software library.

A Cortex-M4 with the FPU is called an M4F. Both M3 and M4 have a three-stage pipeline and full Thumb-2.

Why it matters: audio, motor-control and sensor-fusion code is dominated by multiply-accumulate loops, which is what these additions speed up.

Watch out: on ordinary integer code an M4 runs at about the same speed per MHz as an M3, because the pipeline is the same. The gain shows only in code that uses the new instructions.

cards.title: Which Armv-M architecture version does each core implement: Cortex-M0+, M3, M4, M7, M23, M33, M55 and M85?
cards.body:
M0+: Armv6-M. M3: Armv7-M. M4 and M7: Armv7E-M. M23 and M33: Armv8-M (Baseline and Mainline). M55 and M85: Armv8.1-M Mainline.

An architecture version is the contract between hardware and software: the instructions, registers and memory model. A core is one implementation of it, so many cores can share one version.

- Armv7E-M is Armv7-M plus DSP extensions (so M4 and M7 can run M3 code).
- Armv8-M Baseline is the small, Armv6-M-like profile (M23); Mainline is the fuller, Armv7-M-like profile (M33).
- Armv8.1-M adds the optional **Helium** vector extension (MVE), whose instructions work on 128-bit vectors holding several values at once (M55 and M85).

Watch out: Armv8-M is the microcontroller line, not Armv8-A. The "A" profile is the application-processor family, with 64-bit execution and an MMU for operating systems such as Linux.

cards.title: Example: a connected sensor must keep its cloud credentials safe even if its network code has a bug, and it also runs light floating-point filtering. Of the Cortex-M0+, M4, M23 and M33, which core fits, and which feature protects the credentials?
cards.body:
The Cortex-M33, with TrustZone protecting the credentials and its FPU handling the filtering.

The M33 is an Armv8-M Mainline core whose TrustZone, single-precision FPU and DSP instructions are all options. The M0+ has neither feature, the M4 can have an FPU but never TrustZone, and the M23 can have TrustZone but never an FPU. **TrustZone** for Armv8-M splits memory and CPU state into a Secure world and a Non-secure world in hardware. Non-secure code cannot read Secure memory and can enter Secure code only through defined entry points.

Key idea: keep key storage and crypto in the Secure world and the application and network stack in the Non-secure world. A bug that hijacks the network code still cannot read the keys.

Watch out: TrustZone and the FPU are options the chip designer chooses, so check that the part includes both. M0+, M3, M4 and M7 have no TrustZone at all, and TrustZone isolates software only; it does not stop physical attacks such as probing the chip.

cards.title: Why is the belief "every Cortex-M4 chip has a floating-point unit" false?
cards.body:
The FPU is an optional part of the Cortex-M4 design; the chip maker decides whether to include it, and only parts with it are Cortex-M4F.

Cores such as the M7, M33, M55 and M85 also offer the FPU as an option. A chip with no FPU runs every float operation as a software routine that costs many cycles.

Why it matters: building for the wrong target fails in two ways. Code built to use an FPU that is missing, or one that is present but not yet enabled, faults on the first floating-point instruction. Code built for no FPU on an FPU part works but wastes the hardware.

Tip: read the core line of the exact part's datasheet ("Cortex-M4 with FPU" or not) before choosing build flags. Families from the same vendor can differ, so check each part.

cards.title: How many pipeline stages do the Cortex-M0+, Cortex-M4 and Cortex-M7 have?
cards.body:
Cortex-M0+: 2 stages. Cortex-M4: 3 stages. Cortex-M7: 6 stages.

The Cortex-M3 also has 3 stages. The M7's deeper pipeline lets it clock higher, and it can also issue two instructions per cycle. Its caches and **tightly coupled memory** (fast SRAM wired straight to the core) keep it fed at those speeds, which flash alone could not, so M7 parts run at hundreds of MHz.

Why it matters: a shallower pipeline costs less area and power and loses fewer cycles when a branch flushes it, which suits small cores. A deeper one allows a faster clock, at the cost of more area and a bigger loss on each flush.

Watch out: the stage count belongs to Arm's core design and is the same in every chip built on that core. It does not fix the chip's clock, which also depends on the vendor's silicon process and memory system.

cards.title: Trade-off: a temperature node on a coin cell wakes once a minute, reads one sensor and sends a few bytes. Cortex-M0+ or Cortex-M4F?
cards.body:
Cortex-M0+, because the tiny amount of integer work per wake-up makes sleep current, wake-up time and chip cost matter far more than arithmetic speed.

Over a minute the node is asleep almost all the time, so average power is dominated by sleep current and by how quickly it wakes, does its job and returns to sleep. A small core leaks less and the part costs less.

The other side: if each wake-up filters or transforms data with floating-point math or long multiply-accumulate loops, the M4F can finish in a fraction of the cycles and return to sleep sooner, which can use less energy overall even though its active power is higher.

Watch out: the chip's sleep current, wake-up time and radio usually decide battery life more than the core does, so compare whole parts and their datasheet current figures, not just core names.

cards.title: Trade-off: an always-on keyword spotter runs an int8 model needing about 50 million multiply-accumulates per second. Cortex-M4F or Cortex-M55?
cards.body:
Cortex-M55, because Helium's vector multiply-accumulate finishes the work in far fewer cycles, so the core is busy a much smaller share of the time.

An M4 does at most two 16-bit multiply-accumulates per cycle with its DSP instructions, and in real code load and loop overhead cut that further, so $50\times10^{6}$ MACs per second can keep it busy at a large fraction of a $100\,\mathrm{MHz}$ clock. The M55 can do up to eight 8-bit multiply-accumulates per cycle at peak, so it needs far fewer active cycles.

The other side: if the model is tiny (tens of thousands of MACs per inference) an M4F is idle almost all the time and is cheaper and widely available. Pick the M55 when the workload would keep the M4F busy near full speed, or when you want headroom for a larger model.

Watch out: whole models rarely sustain the peak rates, so compare measured inference time on the actual parts, using optimized library code on both.

cards.title: Trade-off: a battery camera must run an int8 person-detection network several times per second. Cortex-M7 or Cortex-M85?
cards.body:
Cortex-M85 (or M55), because Helium vector instructions do int8 convolutions much faster per MHz than the M7's scalar and 16-bit SIMD instructions.

The deciding factor is the workload: a vision network spends most of its time in convolutions, long runs of int8 multiply-accumulates that map directly onto Helium's wide vectors. Both cores have optional caches and tightly coupled memory, which help with large frame buffers kept in external or on-chip RAM.

The other side: pick the M7 when the network is small enough to meet the frame rate on it and you want the widest choice of parts, mature drivers and tools, or a lower price. M7 parts have been on the market far longer than M85 parts.

Tip: very heavy vision loads often add a separate neural-network accelerator next to the core. Then the core's job is control and pre-processing, and the cheaper core may win.

cards.title: Decode the RISC-V name **RV32IMAC**.
cards.body:
A 32-bit RISC-V core with the base integer instructions (I) plus the extensions M (multiply and divide), A (atomic instructions) and C (16-bit compressed instructions).

An **ISA extension** is an optional, standardized group of instructions named by a letter. The base RV32I has no multiply or divide at all, so small cores add M. Other common letters: F is single-precision floating point and D is double-precision.

Example: RV32IMC is the same core without A. The ESP32-C3 is described as RV32IMC: it multiplies and divides in hardware and has compressed instructions, but no atomics and no FPU.

Watch out: no F means no FPU, so `float` math runs as library code. Match the compiler flags to the chip: `-march=rv32imac -mabi=ilp32` for this core, where `ilp32` is the ABI that uses no floating-point registers.

cards.title: What is **machine mode** in RISC-V?
cards.body:
The highest privilege level (M-mode) and the only one every RISC-V core must have: the core starts in it after reset, and it can access every control register, all memory and all devices.

Small RISC-V MCUs often implement only machine mode, or machine plus user mode. Traps and interrupts go to machine mode by default, so the firmware's trap handler runs there.

Why it matters: it plays the role of an operating system's kernel mode: the level that owns the interrupt and system registers, while the optional user mode runs less trusted code.

Watch out: M-mode uses physical addresses with no MMU translation, and the optional memory-protection feature normally restricts only the lower modes, so a bug in M-mode code can overwrite anything, including the trap handler's own data.

cards.title: What is a **control and status register (CSR)** in RISC-V?
cards.body:
A register in a separate 12-bit address space (4096 possible CSRs) that holds core configuration and trap state, accessed with special instructions such as `csrr`, `csrw`, `csrs` and `csrc` rather than loads and stores.

The CSRs for machine mode include `mstatus` (global interrupt enable), `mie` (which interrupts are enabled), `mtvec` (trap handler address), `mepc` (where the trap happened) and `mcause` (why it happened).

Example: `csrs mstatus, 8` sets bit 3 of `mstatus`, the machine-mode global interrupt enable (MIE), because $8 = 1 \ll 3$. The `csrr rd, csr` form reads one.

Watch out: CSRs are not memory-mapped, so a `volatile` pointer cannot reach them; use inline assembly or compiler intrinsics. This differs from the Cortex-M's interrupt controller (the NVIC) and system control registers, which are memory-mapped.

cards.title: What does RISC-V hardware do when a trap is taken in machine mode, and what are `mtvec` and `mcause`?
cards.body:
It saves the trapped PC in `mepc`, writes the cause to `mcause`, clears the global interrupt enable (`mstatus.MIE`, keeping the old value in `MPIE`) and jumps to the address in `mtvec`; `mret` returns.

`mtvec` is the trap vector base address; its low two bits are the mode. In direct mode (0) every trap goes to the base address. In vectored mode (1) interrupts go to the base plus 4 times the cause number, and exceptions go to the base.

`mcause` has the top bit set for an interrupt and clear for an exception, and the remaining bits give the code (for example 7 is the machine timer interrupt, 11 the machine external interrupt, 2 an illegal instruction).

Watch out: the hardware does not save any general registers. Unlike a Cortex-M, the handler must save and restore everything it uses. For an exception `mepc` points at the trapping instruction, so a handler for `ecall` (the instruction that traps on purpose to request a service) must add 4 to `mepc` before `mret` to skip it. For an interrupt `mepc` points at the interrupted instruction, which has not run yet and runs after `mret`.

cards.title: Trade-off: for hard real-time interrupt response on a small MCU, does a basic RISC-V CLINT plus PLIC setup or the Cortex-M NVIC give lower, more predictable latency out of the box?
cards.body:
The Cortex-M NVIC, because the core and its NVIC vector, prioritize and save registers in hardware, while the basic RISC-V scheme leaves much of that to software.

The **NVIC** (nested vectored interrupt controller) is built into every Cortex-M core: each interrupt has its own vector and priority, a higher-priority interrupt can preempt a lower one, and the core pushes eight registers onto the stack on entry, before the handler's first instruction.

The basic RISC-V arrangement is the **CLINT** (core-local interruptor, for timer and software interrupts) plus the **PLIC** (platform-level interrupt controller), which ranks external interrupts and hands them over one at a time through a claim and complete handshake. Every external interrupt arrives as the same cause (machine external interrupt), so software saves registers, reads the PLIC's claim register to learn which device it was, and dispatches.

The other side: the **CLIC** (core-local interrupt controller), a RISC-V extension still in draft that several vendors already implement in some form, adds per-interrupt levels, preemption and hardware vectoring, and closes much of the gap on chips that have it.

Watch out: latency depends on the specific chip, so compare measured numbers.

cards.title: Trade-off: a Wi-Fi and Bluetooth LE sensor with simple control logic needs a processor. ESP32-C3 (RISC-V) or a Cortex-M4F part?
cards.body:
The ESP32-C3, because it puts Wi-Fi, Bluetooth LE and a RISC-V core on one low-cost chip and the logic needs no floating-point or DSP speed.

The ESP32-C3 has a single 32-bit RISC-V core (RV32IMC) at up to $160\,\mathrm{MHz}$, $400\,\mathrm{KiB}$ of SRAM (Espressif writes 400 KB; 16 KiB of it serves as cache), 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 5 LE. Program flash is a separate die or chip: most modules pair it with external or in-package flash.

A typical Cortex-M4F part has no Wi-Fi, so the design needs a separate radio module and a way to talk to it.

The other side: choose the M4F when the work is float-heavy or DSP-heavy. The ESP32-C3's core has no FPU and no SIMD multiply-accumulate instructions, so that code would run far slower.

Watch out: also compare sleep current, available drivers and the part's availability. The core's ISA is rarely the deciding factor.

cards.title: What are the sixteen core registers of a Cortex-M processor?
cards.body:
R0 to R12 are general-purpose registers, R13 is the stack pointer (SP), R14 is the link register (LR) and R15 is the program counter (PC).

R0 to R7 are the **low registers**, reachable by nearly all 16-bit instructions. R8 to R12 are the **high registers** with more limited access. LR receives the return address on a function call (`bl`), and PC holds the address of the current instruction stream.

Under Arm's calling convention (the ABI), R0 to R3 and R12 are caller-saved (R0 to R3 carry arguments, and R0 returns the result), while R4 to R11 are callee-saved.

Watch out: Cortex-M runs only Thumb code, so an address that code branches to through a register, such as a function pointer or the value in LR, must have bit 0 set to 1. Such a branch to an address with bit 0 clear faults.

Besides these sixteen there are special registers (xPSR, PRIMASK, BASEPRI, FAULTMASK, CONTROL) reached with the `mrs` and `msr` instructions.

cards.title: What is **xPSR** in a Cortex-M, and what do the N, Z, C and V flags mean?
cards.body:
The combined program status register, made of APSR (flags N, Z, C, V, Q), IPSR (current exception number) and EPSR (Thumb bit and execution state); N = negative, Z = zero, C = carry, V = signed overflow.

The flags are bits 31 to 28 of the APSR: N is bit 31, Z bit 30, C bit 29, V bit 28, and bit 27 is Q, a sticky saturation flag set by saturating and DSP instructions.

IPSR is 0 in normal code. Inside a handler it holds the exception number: 15 for SysTick (the core's built-in system timer) and 16 + n for external interrupt n.

Why it matters: conditional branches test these flags. Only flag-setting instructions update them: `adds`, `subs` and `cmp` do, while plain `add` and `sub` do not.

Watch out: C after a subtraction means "no borrow", not "borrow happened".

cards.title: What are **MSP** and **PSP**, and why does an RTOS give tasks the PSP?
cards.body:
Two banked stack pointers behind R13: the main stack pointer (MSP), used from reset and by exception handlers, and the process stack pointer (PSP), which Thread mode may use instead; an RTOS points PSP at the running task's stack and keeps MSP for itself and interrupts.

Normal code runs in **Thread mode** and exception handlers run in **Handler mode**. `CONTROL.SPSEL` picks which stack pointer Thread mode uses; Handler mode always uses MSP. A context switch is then mostly swapping PSP to the next task's stack.

Why: on interrupt entry the hardware pushes the eight-word exception frame onto the stack in use, so it lands on the task's stack (each task stack needs room for it), but the handler itself then runs on MSP, and nested interrupts also push onto MSP. One MSP can be sized for the deepest interrupt nesting, instead of every task reserving that space.

Watch out: separate stacks do not stop a task that overflows its stack from overwriting whatever memory lies next to it. Catching that takes an MPU guard region or, on Armv8-M Mainline cores such as the M33, the stack-limit registers.

cards.title: What are Thread mode and Handler mode in a Cortex-M, and how do privileged and unprivileged execution fit in?
cards.body:
Thread mode runs normal application code and can be privileged or unprivileged (set by `CONTROL.nPRIV`); Handler mode runs exception and interrupt handlers and is always privileged.

After reset the core is in Thread mode, privileged, using MSP. When an exception occurs it switches to Handler mode. Returning from the last active handler goes back to Thread mode; a nested handler returns to the handler it interrupted.

**Privileged** code can use all instructions and registers. **Unprivileged** code is limited: it cannot write most special registers (apart from the APSR flags) or the core's own system control registers, such as the interrupt controller, and the optional memory protection unit can restrict its memory access further.

Why it matters: this is the same user/kernel split an OS uses. An RTOS can run application tasks unprivileged so a stray write cannot disable interrupts or reconfigure the system.

Watch out: privilege and mode are separate. Handler mode is always privileged, but Thread mode is not always unprivileged.

cards.title: Why is the belief "unprivileged code can write `CONTROL` to make itself privileged again" false?
cards.body:
Writes to special registers such as `CONTROL` from unprivileged code are ignored; the only way back to privileged is an exception, whose handler runs privileged and can clear `CONTROL.nPRIV`.

Typically the code executes `svc`, which raises an exception. The handler runs in Handler mode, which is always privileged, and may clear `nPRIV` in `CONTROL` so Thread mode becomes privileged on return.

Why it matters: this is what makes privilege a real protection, like a system call into a kernel. The handler decides what the caller may do.

Watch out: the escalation path itself needs checking. An SVC handler that clears `nPRIV` for any caller defeats the protection.

cards.title:
On a Cortex-M3, what are the N, Z, C and V flags after this code?

```asm
.syntax unified
.thumb
    movs  r0, #1
    subs  r0, r0, #1
```
cards.body:
N = 0, Z = 1, C = 1, V = 0.

`subs` computes $1 - 1 = 0$. The result is zero, so Z = 1, and it is not negative, so N = 0.

Why: on Arm, C after a subtraction means no borrow occurred, which is true when the first operand is at least the second as unsigned numbers. $1 \geq 1$, so C = 1. No signed overflow happens, so V = 0.

Watch out: this is why `cmp r0, r1` followed by `bhs` ("higher or same") branches when C = 1. A programmer expecting C = 1 to mean "borrow" gets unsigned comparisons backwards.

cards.title:
This runs in privileged Thread mode on a Cortex-M3. After `isb`, which stack pointer does `push` use, and is the code still privileged?

```asm
.syntax unified
.thumb
start_task:
    ldr   r0, =task_stack_top
    msr   psp, r0
    movs  r0, #2
    msr   control, r0
    isb
    push  {r4}
```
cards.body:
`push` uses PSP, and the code is still privileged.

`CONTROL` is now $2 = 0b10$. Bit 1 is SPSEL: 1 selects PSP for Thread mode. Bit 0 is nPRIV: 0 means privileged. So only the stack changed.

Why: PSP is loaded first, so the new stack is valid the moment the switch happens. The `isb` (instruction synchronization barrier) is needed after writing `CONTROL` so the change takes effect before later instructions.

Watch out: from this point `r4` goes onto the task's stack. In C, do this in assembly or a naked function (one the compiler emits with no prologue or epilogue): if the compiler had locals on the old stack, they would now be out of reach. To make the task unprivileged too, write 3 instead of 2.

cards.title:
A Cortex-M4's interrupt controller implements 4 priority bits, kept in the top 4 bits of each 8-bit priority value (so levels are `0x00`, `0x10`, ... `0xF0`). Smaller numbers are more urgent. After this code, which interrupts can still preempt?

```asm
.syntax unified
.thumb
    movs  r0, #0x40
    msr   basepri, r0
```
cards.body:
Only interrupts with priority value below `0x40`: levels `0x00`, `0x10`, `0x20` and `0x30`, the four most urgent of the 16.

When `BASEPRI` is nonzero, it blocks every interrupt whose priority value is equal to or larger than it (equal or less urgent). Interrupts with level `0x40` and above are held off until `BASEPRI` is set back to 0.

Why it matters: RTOS kernels use `BASEPRI` for critical sections so that the most urgent interrupts, which must not call kernel functions, keep running. `PRIMASK` is the blunt tool: setting it to 1 blocks all interrupts except NMI (a non-maskable interrupt) and HardFault (the core's catch-all fault exception).

Watch out: `BASEPRI` exists on Armv7-M cores (M3, M4, M7) but not on Cortex-M0 and M0+.

cards.title: What is a **memory map**, and how does the Cortex-M's 4 GiB address space divide into regions?
cards.body:
The fixed assignment of address ranges to memories and peripherals; in a Cortex-M: Code `0x00000000`, SRAM `0x20000000`, Peripheral `0x40000000`, External RAM `0x60000000`, External device `0xA0000000`, System `0xE0000000`.

The **address space** is every address the core can produce. A 32-bit core has $2^{32}$ bytes, which is 4 GiB. The regions are 512 MiB (Code), 512 MiB (SRAM), 512 MiB (Peripheral), 1 GiB (External RAM), 1 GiB (External device) and 512 MiB (System, which holds the private peripheral bus at `0xE0000000` and vendor-specific space above it).

Why it matters: the CPU reaches flash, RAM and peripherals with the same load and store instructions, and the address alone decides which one answers.

Watch out: the generic map says which kind of thing belongs where. The actual flash size and base, SRAM size and peripheral addresses come from the vendor's memory-map table. An access to an address nothing answers causes a bus fault.

cards.title: What are a **peripheral base address** and a **register offset**, and how do they give a register's address?
cards.body:
The base address is where a peripheral's register block starts and the offset is a register's distance in bytes from it; register address = base address + offset.

A vendor's memory-map table lists each peripheral's base address, and the peripheral's register map lists each register's offset.

Example: on the STM32F407, GPIOD has base `0x40020C00` and its output data register (ODR) has offset `0x14`, so ODR is at `0x40020C14`.

Watch out: offsets are in bytes, not register numbers. Registers are usually 4 bytes apart, so the sixth register has offset `0x14`, not 6. In C a struct overlay gives the same result: the address of a member is the base plus the member's byte offset in the struct, which the `offsetof` macro from `<stddef.h>` returns.

cards.title: What are the **Private Peripheral Bus (PPB)** and the **System Control Space (SCS)**?
cards.body:
The PPB is the 1 MiB region at `0xE0000000` holding the core's own debug, trace and system blocks; the SCS, starting at `0xE000E000`, holds SysTick, the NVIC, the System Control Block and the MPU registers.

Inside the SCS: SysTick at `0xE000E010`, the NVIC at `0xE000E100`, the System Control Block (SCB) at `0xE000ED00` and the MPU at `0xE000ED90`.

Key idea: these registers belong to the core, not to the vendor, so they sit at the same addresses on every Cortex-M3 or M4 chip, and the core reaches them over its own bus.

Watch out: the vendor's reference manual does not describe them. Look in Arm's documentation for the core. Only privileged code can access them.

**Endianness** is the order in which a multi-byte value's bytes sit in memory. Little-endian stores the least significant byte at the lowest address, so `p[0]` is `0x78` and `p[3]` is `0x12`.

Why it matters: Cortex-M devices run little-endian in practice (the architecture allows a big-endian build chosen at reset, but it is rare). cards.title: How does **bit-banding** let a Cortex-M3 or M4 change a single bit atomically?
cards.body:
Each bit in the lowest 1 MiB of the SRAM and peripheral regions has its own 32-bit alias word in a 32 MiB region above; writing 0 or 1 to that word changes just that bit in one atomic access. Alias address = alias base + byte offset × 32 + bit number × 4.

The bit-band regions: SRAM `0x20000000` to `0x200FFFFF` with alias `0x22000000` to `0x23FFFFFF`; peripherals `0x40000000` to `0x400FFFFF` with alias `0x42000000` to `0x43FFFFFF`. The sizes match: $1\,\mathrm{MiB} \times 8$ bits $\times\ 4$ bytes $= 32\,\mathrm{MiB}$.

Why it works: the bus hardware turns a write to the alias word into an indivisible read-modify-write of the real byte, so an interrupt cannot slip in between. Only the least significant bit of the written value matters, and a read returns 0 or 1.

Watch out: bit-banding exists only on Cortex-M3 and M4 parts whose vendor implemented it. Cortex-M0+, M7 and the Armv8-M cores do not have it.

cards.title: A reference manual's memory map lists GPIOD at base `0x40020C00`; its register map lists BSRR at offset `0x18`. Bits 0 to 15 of BSRR set the matching output pins when written as 1, and bits 16 to 31 clear them; writing 0 does nothing. (a) At what address do you write? (b) What value sets pin PD12 without touching other pins?
cards.body:
Write to `0x40020C18`; the value `0x00001000` sets PD12 (the value `0x10000000` would clear it).

Address: base + offset $=$ `0x40020C00` + `0x18` $=$ `0x40020C18`.

Value: PD12 is pin 12 of the port, so the set bit is bit 12: $1 \ll 12 =$ `0x1000`. The clear bit for the same pin is bit $12 + 16 = 28$: $1 \ll 28 =$ `0x10000000`. All other bits are 0, which BSRR ignores.

Why it works: because zeros have no effect, one write changes exactly one pin, with no need to read the output register first.

Watch out: use plain assignment such as `GPIOD->BSRR = 1u << 12;`, not `|=`. BSRR is write-only, so a read-modify-write on it is meaningless and would be wrong on any register whose read value differs from what was written.

`0x22006008`

Alias address $=$ alias base $+$ byte offset $\times 32 +$ bit $\times 4$.

- Byte offset from the SRAM base: `0x20000300` $-$ `0x20000000` $=$ `0x300` $= 768$.
- $768 \times 32 = 24{,}576 =$ `0x6000`.
- Bit 2: $2 \times 4 = 8 =$ `0x8`.
- Total: `0x22000000` $+$ `0x6000` $+$ `0x8` $=$ `0x22006008`.

Writing 1 to that word sets bit 2 of the byte at `0x20000300`, for example with `*(volatile uint32_t *)0x22006008u = 1;`.

cards.title: Trade-off: an interrupt handler and the main loop each set and clear different pins of the same GPIO output register. Do you use `ODR |= mask`, a bit-band alias, or the BSRR set/reset register?
cards.body:
The BSRR set/reset register, because it changes only the pins you name in one write, so it is atomic and works on every core.

`ODR |= mask` is a read-modify-write: if the interrupt changes a different pin between the read and the write, the main loop's write puts back the old value and the interrupt's change is lost. This is a race condition.

A bit-band alias write is also atomic, but only for one bit at a time, only on M3 and M4 parts that implement it, and only in the lowest 1 MiB of a region. Use it when the register has no set/reset pair, for example a flag byte in SRAM shared with an interrupt.

Another fix is to disable interrupts around the read-modify-write, which costs interrupt latency.

Tip: prefer hardware set/clear registers. They also survive a move from an M4 to an M7 or M33, which have no bit-banding.

cards.title: What is **flash memory**, and why must a **page** be erased before it is rewritten?
cards.body:
Non-volatile memory that keeps its contents without power; on most MCUs an erase sets every bit in a page (or sector) to 1 and programming can only change 1s to 0s, so rewriting needs a **page erase** first.

A page is the smallest erase unit: from a few hundred bytes on some parts to sectors of 128 KiB or more on others, depending on the chip. On those parts erased flash reads as all ones (`0xFF` in each byte).

Why it matters: flash reads are fast enough to execute code in place, but writes are slow and the erase unit is coarse. To change one byte in a stored settings block, you must save the page, erase it and program it again.

Watch out: on many MCUs, while a flash bank is being erased or programmed the CPU stalls on any read from that bank. Code that must keep running (such as a motor control interrupt) should live in SRAM during the operation or in the other bank.

cards.title: What is **SRAM**, and how does it differ from flash inside an MCU?
cards.body:
Volatile static RAM: it loses its contents without power, but reads and writes, usually at full core speed, with no erase step and effectively unlimited write cycles.

SRAM holds the stack, heap, global variables and buffers. It is small (a few KiB to about a megabyte on most MCUs) because every bit takes several transistors, and it is kept on-chip beside the core.

Key idea: the MCU **memory hierarchy** is short. From fastest to slowest: registers, optional cache or tightly coupled memory on bigger cores, on-chip SRAM, on-chip flash, then optional external memory. There is usually no DRAM.

Watch out: the program and its constants live in flash, but writable variables must live in SRAM. The startup code copies initial values for globals from flash to SRAM and zeroes the bss, which costs both memories.

cards.title: What is a **wait state** in a memory access?
cards.body:
An extra clock cycle the CPU waits for a memory access to complete because the memory cannot respond within one clock period.

Flash needs a fixed time to deliver data, so as the clock gets faster the same time spans more cycles. The number of wait states is $\lceil t_{\text{access}} / T_{\text{clk}} \rceil - 1$, where $T_{\text{clk}}$ is the clock period, and it is set in a flash access-control register.

Example: with a flash that needs $20\,\mathrm{ns}$, a $50\,\mathrm{MHz}$ clock ($T = 20\,\mathrm{ns}$) needs 0 wait states, but a $100\,\mathrm{MHz}$ clock ($T = 10\,\mathrm{ns}$) needs $\lceil 2 \rceil - 1 = 1$.

Watch out: when raising the clock, raise the wait states first; when lowering it, lower the clock first and the wait states after. The reverse order can read flash too fast and crash.

cards.title: What are the AHB, the APB and the bus matrix in an MCU, and why is a peripheral on the APB slower to reach than SRAM?
cards.body:
The AHB is the fast, pipelined bus for the CPU, DMA, memories and fast peripherals; the APB is a simple, low-power bus for ordinary peripherals, reached through a bridge; the bus matrix lets several masters reach different slaves at the same time.

AHB stands for Advanced High-performance Bus and APB for Advanced Peripheral Bus; both are Arm bus standards. A **master** (CPU, DMA) starts transfers; a **slave** (SRAM, flash, a peripheral) answers. The bus matrix is a crossbar that arbitrates: the CPU can fetch from flash while the DMA writes SRAM, and a master waits only if two want the same slave.

An APB transfer is not pipelined, takes at least two APB clock cycles, and passes through the AHB-to-APB bridge. The APB is also usually clocked slower than the AHB (on an STM32F407 at $168\,\mathrm{MHz}$: APB1 at most $42\,\mathrm{MHz}$, APB2 at most $84\,\mathrm{MHz}$).

Watch out: a load that takes a cycle or two from SRAM can take many cycles from an APB register. Avoid tight polling loops on APB registers, and let DMA move bulk data.

cards.title: Why is the belief "doubling the clock doubles how fast code runs from flash" false?
cards.body:
Flash access time does not shrink with the clock, so a faster clock needs more wait states; prefetch buffers and small caches hide part of that, so the speedup is usually smaller than the clock ratio.

A **prefetch buffer** reads a wide chunk of flash (for example 128 bits) ahead of the CPU, so straight-line code pays the wait only once per chunk. A branch or a data read from flash breaks the pattern and pays the full wait.

Example: the STM32F407 needs 0 wait states up to $30\,\mathrm{MHz}$ and 5 at $168\,\mathrm{MHz}$ (at $2.7$ to $3.6\,\mathrm{V}$): each flash read takes 6 cycles instead of 1. ST's flash accelerator (prefetch plus small instruction and data caches) exists to claw most of that back.

Watch out: benchmark on your own code. Loops that fit the cache run nearly at full clock speed, while branchy code or reads of constant tables in flash run much slower than the MHz figure suggests.

cards.title: About how many erase cycles can a typical on-chip MCU flash page endure?
cards.body:
About $10{,}000$ erase cycles (a datasheet figure of 10 kcycles); some parts rate $100{,}000$.

Write endurance is the number of erase-and-program cycles a page is guaranteed to survive. For example, the STM32F412 datasheet quotes 10 kcycles over its temperature range, and its data retention figure is $30$ years at $85\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ after only 1 kcycle. Retention shortens as cycles and temperature rise.

Example: rewriting a settings record in the same page once per second (an erase and a program each time) reaches $10{,}000$ erases in $10{,}000\,\mathrm{s}$, under $3$ hours. Spreading the writes evenly over 100 pages (**wear leveling**) stretches that to about $11.6$ days.

Watch out: endurance counts erases of a page, not writes to a byte. Check the datasheet's memory characteristics table for your part, and store frequently changed data in SRAM, a small dedicated memory, or a log that rotates across pages.

cards.body:
2 wait states; zero wait states up to about $41.7\,\mathrm{MHz}$.

Clock period at $120\,\mathrm{MHz}$: $T = 1/120\,\mathrm{MHz} \approx 8.33\,\mathrm{ns}$.

Cycles needed: $\lceil 24 / 8.33 \rceil = \lceil 2.88 \rceil = 3$ cycles per read, which is 1 normal cycle plus 2 wait states.

Zero wait states means the access fits in one period: $T \geq 24\,\mathrm{ns}$, so $f \leq 1/24\,\mathrm{ns} \approx 41.7\,\mathrm{MHz}$.

Watch out: this assumes whole-cycle accesses and ignores prefetch. Real parts publish a table of wait states per frequency band and supply voltage; follow that table, not a calculation. Check also that 2.88 rounds up (never down): rounding down gives a read that finishes after the CPU has already sampled the data.

cards.title: A part has $512\,\mathrm{KiB}$ of flash and $128\,\mathrm{KiB}$ of SRAM. The firmware without the model uses $140\,\mathrm{KiB}$ of flash and $20\,\mathrm{KiB}$ of SRAM (globals, heap, stack). An int8 network has $230\,\mathrm{KiB}$ of weights and needs a $70\,\mathrm{KiB}$ tensor arena for activations. Does it fit, where does each part live, and what is left of each memory?
cards.body:
It fits: flash $370$ of $512\,\mathrm{KiB}$ used ($142$ free), SRAM $90$ of $128\,\mathrm{KiB}$ used ($38$ free); weights in flash, tensor arena in SRAM.

Weights are constant, so they are placed in flash and read in place. The tensor arena holds intermediate activations that change on every inference, so it must be in SRAM.

- Flash: $140 + 230 = 370\,\mathrm{KiB}$; $512 - 370 = 142\,\mathrm{KiB}$ free.
- SRAM: $20 + 70 = 90\,\mathrm{KiB}$; $128 - 90 = 38\,\mathrm{KiB}$ free.

Watch out: if the product needs a second complete firmware image for safe updates, flash needs $2 \times 370 = 740\,\mathrm{KiB}$, which does not fit. Check that headroom for your plan before committing to a part.

cards.title: Trade-off: on a Cortex-M7, do you place a control-loop interrupt's code and data in tightly coupled memory (TCM) or rely on the caches?
cards.body:
TCM, when you need hard, repeatable timing for a small, known set of hot code and data; caches when the working set is large or you cannot predict what will be hot.

**Tightly coupled memory** is SRAM wired directly to the core over a dedicated port (ITCM for instructions, DTCM for data). Accesses never miss and take a fixed small number of cycles, so memory timing does not change from run to run.

A cache is automatic, but a miss can cost many cycles, so the same code can take different times: jitter in the loop. When a DMA engine writes memory that is also cached, the cache may keep stale data, so you must clean or invalidate it in software.

The other side: TCM is small and you place code and data in it by hand, using the linker. Large programs and big buffers go to normal SRAM or flash behind the caches.

Tip: put the interrupt handlers, the stack of time-critical code and the data they touch in TCM; leave everything else to the caches.

cards.title: Trade-off: keep int8 model weights in flash and read them in place, or copy them into SRAM at boot?
cards.body:
Read them in place from flash when SRAM is scarce, which is the usual case; copy them to SRAM (or TCM) only if SRAM is plentiful and flash reads are the bottleneck.

Weights are read-only and read in order, so prefetching and the flash accelerator serve them well. Flash is also far larger than SRAM, and weights rarely fit in SRAM next to the activations and stack.

The other side: SRAM has no wait states and no stalls. If the model is slow because reads of weights from flash or slow external flash dominate, copying them into fast memory can speed inference up noticeably. Weights stored in external serial flash may need a copy to fast internal memory.

Watch out: a copy costs SRAM equal to the whole weight set, plus boot time to copy it. Compare the weights' size with what is left after activations, buffers and stack, as in a memory-budget table.

cards.title: What is a **clock tree** in a microcontroller?
cards.body:
The network that takes clock sources (an internal RC oscillator, an external crystal), optionally multiplies them in a PLL, selects the system clock (SYSCLK) and divides it with prescalers into the clocks for the core, the buses and each peripheral.

An **oscillator** is a circuit that makes a repeating signal. A **crystal** is a quartz part that sets an oscillator's frequency very precisely. A **PLL** (phase-locked loop) multiplies a clock up to a higher frequency. A **prescaler** divides a clock by a fixed ratio. **SYSCLK** is the main clock that feeds the core and the buses.

Example (STM32F407): internal RC at $16\,\mathrm{MHz}$ or an external crystal feeds the PLL, which produces SYSCLK of up to $168\,\mathrm{MHz}$. An AHB prescaler gives the core and bus clock, and the APB buses sit behind two more prescalers (at most $42\,\mathrm{MHz}$ and $84\,\mathrm{MHz}$).

Tip: the clock-tree diagram in the reference manual is the first thing to read when bringing up a chip. Every branch has its own maximum frequency, and each peripheral has its own clock gate.

cards.title: What is **clock gating** of peripherals, and what happens if you forget to enable a peripheral's clock?
cards.body:
Each peripheral's clock has an enable bit; with the clock off the block is frozen and its registers do not respond (on an STM32, writes are lost and reads usually return 0), so you must set the enable bit first.

Why: a frozen block does not switch, so its dynamic power (activity factor times switched capacitance times $V^2 f$) drops to nearly zero. Chips therefore start with most peripheral clocks off.

Example (STM32): `RCC->AHB1ENR |= RCC_AHB1ENR_GPIODEN;` turns on the GPIOD clock, after which `GPIOD->MODER` and other registers respond.

Watch out: the classic "nothing happens" bug is configuring a peripheral before enabling its clock. On some families a short delay is needed after enabling, and reading the enable register back once is a common way to provide it.

cards.title: Name the common MCU **reset sources**.
cards.body:
Power-on reset, brown-out reset, watchdog reset, the external reset pin and software reset.

- **Power-on reset (POR):** the supply rises from zero past a threshold.
- **Brown-out reset (BOR):** the supply falls below a set threshold while running, so the chip holds reset instead of executing at too low a voltage.
- **Watchdog:** a timer that software must refresh regularly; if it expires, the chip resets, which recovers from hangs.
- **Pin:** the reset input is pulled low (button, debugger).
- **Software:** firmware requests a reset (on Cortex-M by setting the `SYSRESETREQ` bit in the AIRCR register, in a write whose top half carries the key `0x05FA`, or the write is ignored).

After any reset a Cortex-M loads the initial MSP from the first word of the vector table (the table of addresses at the start of the program image) and the reset handler's address (PC) from the second.

Tip: read the chip's reset-status flags at startup and log which source fired. A watchdog or brown-out reset in the field is a bug report.

cards.title: How does a **PLL** turn an $8\,\mathrm{MHz}$ crystal into a $168\,\mathrm{MHz}$ system clock?
cards.body:
A phase-locked loop (PLL) steers an internal voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) until a divided copy of its output matches the reference clock, so the output is the reference times a ratio.

Crystals top out at tens of MHz, but a PLL's feedback loop forces its faster oscillator to stay in step with the crystal, so the output keeps the crystal's accuracy. On an STM32F4 the ratio comes from three integer settings: an input divider, a multiplier and an output divider.

The PLL takes time to lock, typically tens to hundreds of microseconds, and its VCO works only within a specified frequency range.

Watch out: set the flash wait states first, then wait for the PLL's "ready" flag before switching SYSCLK to it. Too few wait states at the new speed make the core read wrong data from flash and crash. The STM32F4 holds off a switch to a PLL that is not ready yet, but not every chip does.

cards.title: For an STM32F4-style PLL with input clock $f_{in}$, input divider $M$, multiplier $N$ and output divider $P$, what is the system clock, and what limits the VCO?
cards.body:
$f_{\text{SYSCLK}} = f_{in} \cdot \dfrac{N}{M \cdot P}$, where the VCO runs at $f_{in} \cdot N / M$.

On the STM32F4 the VCO input $f_{in}/M$ must be $1$ to $2\,\mathrm{MHz}$ and the VCO output $f_{in} N / M$ must be $100$ to $432\,\mathrm{MHz}$. $P$ is one of 2, 4, 6 or 8.

Example: with $f_{in} = 8\,\mathrm{MHz}$, $M = 8$, $N = 336$, $P = 2$: VCO input $= 1\,\mathrm{MHz}$, VCO output $= 336\,\mathrm{MHz}$ and $f_{\text{SYSCLK}} = 168\,\mathrm{MHz}$.

Watch out: the field names $M$, $N$ and $P$ and their limits are those of the STM32F4 family. Other chips name and limit them differently, and some add a fractional multiplier, so use the reference manual's formula for your part.

$M = 25$, $N = 336$, $P = 2$.

Work from the constraints. The VCO output must equal $168 \cdot P$ and stay at or below $432\,\mathrm{MHz}$, so $P = 2$ ($336\,\mathrm{MHz}$) works, while $P = 4$ would need $672\,\mathrm{MHz}$, which is out of range.

Check: $25 \cdot 336 / (25 \cdot 2) = 168\,\mathrm{MHz}$. Both limits hold.

cards.title: A real-time clock counts seconds from a **32.768 kHz RTC crystal**. How many seconds per day can it drift if the crystal is accurate to $\pm 20\,\mathrm{ppm}$, compared with a clock from an on-chip RC oscillator accurate to $\pm 2\%$?
cards.body:
At most about $1.73\,\mathrm{s}$ per day for the crystal, versus about $1{,}728\,\mathrm{s}$ (28.8 minutes) per day for the RC.

The crystal's frequency, $32{,}768 = 2^{15}$ Hz, is chosen so a chain of 15 divide-by-2 stages yields exactly 1 Hz, which is why it is the standard RTC part.

$20\,\mathrm{ppm}$ means 20 parts per million, a fractional error of $20 \times 10^{-6}$. Over a day of $86{,}400\,\mathrm{s}$: $86{,}400 \times 20 \times 10^{-6} = 1.728\,\mathrm{s}$.

For $\pm 2\%$: $86{,}400 \times 0.02 = 1{,}728\,\mathrm{s}$.

Watch out: these are worst-case tolerance bounds for a constant error. Real crystals also drift with temperature and with the load capacitors on the board, but they remain far better than an RC oscillator, which is why RTCs use a crystal.

cards.title: Trade-off: a cost-sensitive node has only a UART at 115200 baud and no USB or radio. Should the main clock come from the internal RC oscillator or an external crystal?
cards.body:
The internal RC oscillator, if its worst-case error over temperature and supply voltage stays inside what the UART tolerates, because that saves a crystal, two capacitors and board space and the chip starts up faster.

A UART has no clock wire: the receiver times each bit from the start edge and samples near the middle. Its **baud** rate is its bit rate, here 115,200 bits per second. For 8N1 framing (start bit, 8 data bits, stop bit) the stop bit is sampled about 9.5 bit times after the start edge, and the sample must stay within half a bit, so the combined error of both ends must be below about $0.5/9.5 \approx 5\%$. A common rule of thumb keeps the total within about 2%, because noise, edge distortion and the receiver's sampling steps eat into that margin.

The other side: choose a crystal when something needs accuracy. USB full speed requires a clock within about $0.25\%$, radios have tight frequency limits, and timekeeping needs the ppm-level accuracy of a crystal.

Watch out: an RC oscillator's error includes drift with temperature and voltage, not only the factory-calibrated figure at room temperature.

cards.title: What does the Cortex-M4 DSP instruction **SMLAD** do?
cards.body:
`SMLAD Rd, Rn, Rm, Ra` computes Rd = Ra + Rn[15:0] × Rm[15:0] + Rn[31:16] × Rm[31:16]: two signed 16-bit multiply-accumulates in one instruction, which takes one cycle on the M4.

This is **SIMD** (single instruction, multiple data): one instruction works on several values packed into one 32-bit register. Here each register holds two 16-bit samples, so one `LDR` fetches two values and one SMLAD uses them.

Key idea: a dot product of $n$ pairs of int16 values needs only about $n/2$ SMLADs. CMSIS, Arm's standard software layer for Cortex-M, provides it as the intrinsic `__SMLAD()`. The accumulator is 32 bits wide, so long sums of large products can overflow it; the Q flag is set if the final add overflows.

Why it matters: **Helium** (the vector extension on Cortex-M55 and M85) widens this idea to 128-bit vectors: 16 int8, 8 int16 or 4 int32 lanes per instruction.

Watch out: SMLAD is not on Cortex-M0+ or M3; it is part of the DSP extension.

cards.title: Why is double-precision math slow on a Cortex-M4F?
cards.body:
The M4F's FPU handles only single precision (32-bit `float`), so every `double` operation becomes a call to a software library routine that costs tens to hundreds of cycles.

A **single-precision** value is the 32-bit IEEE 754 float format. The FPU does an add or multiply on it in a few cycles. For 64-bit values there is no hardware at all on an M4F (some Cortex-M7 parts do offer a double-precision FPU).

Example: in C, `0.1` is a `double`. For `float a`, `float y = a * 0.1;` converts `a` to double, multiplies in software and converts the result back to float. Compiled for an M4F, it calls three library routines (`__aeabi_f2d`, `__aeabi_dmul`, `__aeabi_d2f`), while `a * 0.1f` is a single `vmul.f32`.

Watch out: `printf("%f", x)` also converts a `float` to double. Use `f` suffixes, `sinf` rather than `sin`, and consider GCC's option `-fsingle-precision-constant`.

`0xF`

Each coprocessor gets a 2-bit field, and `0b11` means full access. CP10 is bits 21:20 and CP11 is bits 23:22, so setting both gives `0b1111`, which is `0xF`, shifted up to bit 20.

Why it matters: after reset the access is off. So this runs very early, usually in the startup or system-init function, before any floating-point code.

cards.title: Two vectors of 256 Q15 (int16) values are stored as packed pairs in 32-bit words. A Cortex-M4 loop uses one SMLAD per pair of words. How many SMLADs and how many MACs does it perform, and what is the minimum time at $80\,\mathrm{MHz}$ if each SMLAD takes one cycle and all other overhead is ignored?
cards.body:
128 SMLADs, 256 MACs, at least $1.6\,\mu\mathrm{s}$.

Each 32-bit word holds two int16 values, so 256 values take $256/2 = 128$ words per vector. One SMLAD multiplies two pairs and adds both, so 128 SMLADs perform $128 \times 2 = 256$ MACs. At one cycle each, that is 128 cycles: $128 / 80 \times 10^{6} = 1.6\,\mu\mathrm{s}$.

This is a lower bound. Real loops also load two words per SMLAD and count the loop, so the loop is slower. That is why optimized library kernels unroll and schedule loads.

Watch out: the accumulator is 32 bits. A Q15 product is up to $2^{30}$, so a sum of 256 products could reach about $2^{38}$ in the worst case, far past the 32-bit limit of $2^{31}$. For a guarantee, scale the inputs down or use SMLALD, the same dual multiply into a 64-bit accumulator, which gives more guard bits.

294,912 MACs, about $3.7\,\mathrm{ms}$.

Each output value needs $K \times K \times C_{in} = 3 \times 3 \times 8 = 72$ MACs. There are $16 \times 16 \times 16 = 4096$ output values, so $4096 \times 72 = 294{,}912$ MACs.

Time: $294{,}912 / (80 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{MACs/s}) = 3.69\,\mathrm{ms}$. In operations (one MAC counts as 2) that is $589{,}824$.

cards.title: Trade-off: on a Cortex-M4F, do you run a small neural network in float32 on the FPU, or quantize it to int8 and use SIMD integer kernels?
cards.body:
Quantize to int8 when flash, SRAM or speed is tight, which is usual on an MCU; keep float32 only when accuracy or development time matters more and the model is small.

**CMSIS-DSP** is Arm's library of optimized signal-processing routines (filters, FFTs, matrix math), and **CMSIS-NN** is Arm's library of optimized neural-network kernels, mainly for int8. They use the M4's SIMD instructions such as SMLAD.

int8 weights take one quarter the memory of float32 and the SIMD kernels do more MACs per instruction, so both memory and time improve.

The other side: quantization needs calibration data and loses some accuracy, and an unusually wide range of values can hurt int8 more than float. Float32 on the FPU needs no conversion work, so it suits early prototypes and tiny models.

Watch out: measure accuracy on your own test data after quantizing; do not assume it is unchanged.

cards.title: What are an MCU's **datasheet** and **reference manual**, and what does each cover?
cards.body:
The datasheet gives the electrical and physical facts of a part (pinout, packages, absolute maximum ratings, electrical characteristics, memory sizes); the reference manual explains how the chip's blocks and registers work for the whole family (register map, bit fields, reset values).

The **pinout** is the table of which signal each pin carries, including the **alternate functions** a pin can be switched to. **Electrical characteristics** are the guaranteed voltages, currents and timings. The **register map** lists every register's offset and its **reset value**, the value it holds right after reset. One datasheet often covers a few closely related part numbers, which differ in flash size or package.

Why it matters: a question about "how much current does it draw in sleep" goes to the datasheet; "which bit starts the ADC" goes to the reference manual. A third document, the errata sheet, lists known silicon bugs.

Tip: keep both open when writing drivers. The datasheet tells you which pin and peripheral to use, and the reference manual tells you the register bits. Not every vendor splits them this way: Microchip's AVR and SAM datasheets, for example, include the register descriptions too.

cards.title: In a reference manual's register description, what does the access type **w1c** mean?
cards.body:
Write-1-to-clear: writing a 1 to that bit clears it, and writing a 0 leaves it unchanged.

Other common access types are `rw` (read and write), `r` (read-only) and `w` (write-only). Status flags are often w1c, so software can clear exactly the flags it has handled by writing 1s to just those bits, without reading first.

Example: if bits 0 and 1 of a flag register are both set and are w1c, writing `0x1` clears bit 0 and leaves bit 1 set.

Watch out: manuals differ in the labels they use (for example `rc_w1` or `rc_w0` for "read, clear by writing 1 or 0"). Always read the legend at the start of the register chapter before trusting a three-letter code.

cards.title: Example: your SPI (a clocked serial bus) transfers sometimes lose the last byte, and the errata sheet has a matching entry for your chip. What do you do with it?
cards.body:
Check whether the entry applies to your silicon revision, then apply its workaround and re-test.

An **errata sheet** lists known silicon bugs. Each entry gives the symptom, the conditions, the affected revisions and a workaround. The revision is marked on the package or can be read from the chip's ID register (on STM32, the revision ID in `DBGMCU_IDCODE`).

Example entry (made up): "SPI loses the last byte when DMA is used above $20\,\mathrm{MHz}$; workaround: keep the SPI clock at or below $20\,\mathrm{MHz}$ or end the transfer with a software read." If your chip is an affected revision, apply that, document it in the code and re-run the test that failed.

Watch out: you cannot fix a silicon bug in software, only avoid it. A workaround often trades speed or power, so note that cost in the design.

The first blank is 2 (`0b10`, alternate function mode); the second is 7 (AF7).

Pin 2 sits at bits 5:4 of MODER ($2 \times 2 = 4$) and bits 11:8 of AFRL ($2 \times 4 = 8$). MODER value 2 hands the pin to a peripheral, and the AFRL value 7 chooses which peripheral: the datasheet's table says AF7 on PA2 is USART2_TX.

Key idea: the two documents work together. The datasheet says which function is on which pin (AF number), and the reference manual says which register bits to write.

Watch out: enable the GPIOA clock first, or these writes are ignored, and enable the USART2 clock before setting up the USART itself.

cards.title: Trade-off: sizing the regulator for an MCU board, do you use the datasheet's typical or maximum supply-current figure?
cards.body:
The maximum, which is guaranteed over temperature, voltage and part-to-part variation; use typical values only for estimating average battery life.

Electrical-characteristics tables give minimum, typical and maximum columns. Typical is what a normal chip does at room temperature and nominal supply, while the maximum is the most any chip of that type is guaranteed to draw under the stated conditions. Current rises with temperature and clock speed.

A regulator sized on typical current can overload on a hot day with a high-current part. Size it on the maximum, plus the peak currents of peripherals and I/O pins you drive.

The other side: for battery life, the maximum is too pessimistic. Use typical figures at the expected temperature, then leave margin.

Watch out: read the table's conditions (clock, enabled peripherals, voltage, temperature). Also, absolute maximum ratings are damage limits, not operating values; stay inside the recommended operating conditions.
